parole.significato: rhombus (parallelogram having all sides of equal length)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos). Doublet of rumb.
Inherited from Old Catalan roncar, from Latin rhonchāre, a verb based on rhonchus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos, “snoring”).
Inherited from Latin saccus.
Borrowed from Latin sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros).
Borrowed from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα (salamándra).
From Latin salpa, from Ancient Greek σάλπη (sálpē, “a species of fish”).

parole.significato: samfaina, a dish made from tomato, bell pepper, onion, garlic, eggplant, zucchini, fried in olive oil with parsley and…
parole.testo: First attested written in this form in 1890. Inherited from Old Catalan sanfoina, with 19th century interference from the suffix -aina, from Latin symphōnia, originally from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Doublet of simfonia and samfoina.
Learned borrowing from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos).
Borrowed from Latin satrapīa, from Ancient Greek σατραπεία (satrapeía), from σατράπης (satrápēs). By surface analysis, sàtrapa + -ia.
Borrowed from Latin selēnītēs, from Ancient Greek σεληνῑ́της (selēnī́tēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīta, from Ancient Greek Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin sȳcophanta (“informer, trickster”), from Ancient Greek συκοφάντης (sukophántēs).
From Latin sȳcophantia, from Ancient Greek σῡκοφᾰντῐ́ᾱ (sūkophăntĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Latin symmetria (“symmetry”), from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría, “symmetry”), from σύμμετρος (súmmetros, “symmetrical”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).
Borrowed from Latin symphōnia.
Borrowed from Latin syntaxis, from Ancient Greek σῠ́ντᾰξῐς (sŭ́ntăxĭs).
Borrowed from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with”) + ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă, “name”) + -ος (-os).
From Latin Syrius, from Ancient Greek Σύριος (Súrios).
Borrowed from Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).
Inherited from Latin saurellus, diminutive of saurus from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “horse mackerel”).
Inherited from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שבת (shabát, “Sabbath”).

Borrowed from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāwan- (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.
Borrowed from Latin sēpia. Doublet of sípia.
Borrowed from Latin syllaba, from Ancient Greek συλλαβή (sullabḗ), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).
Borrowed from Latin symbolus, from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon).
Learned borrowing from Latin syndicus, from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate”).
From Latin synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos).
Borrowed from Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”).
Borrowed from Latin sēpia.
Borrowed from Latin talentum, from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton).
Borrowed from Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”).
Borrowed from Latin thēca (“case, envelope, sheath”), from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē).
Borrowed from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
Borrowed from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). Equivalent to teo- + -logia.
Borrowed from Latin theōria, from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría).
Borrowed from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos).
Inherited from Latin taeda.
Borrowed from Latin theologus, from Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos).
Borrowed from Latin tīgris, from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris).
Borrowed from Latin thymus.
Borrowed from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos).
Borrowed from Latin tyrannus, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “absolute ruler”).
From Latin tisana, from Ancient Greek πτισάνη (ptisánē).
Borrowed from Latin phthisis, from Ancient Greek φθῐ́σῐς (phthĭ́sĭs).
Borrowed from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). First attested in 1575.
Borrowed from Latin topazius, from Ancient Greek τόπαζος (tópazos).
Inherited from Old Catalan torre~torra, from Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis).

Borrowed from Latin triumphus (“triumphal procession”), ultimately from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos, “thriambus”). Doublet of trumfo. Triomf was originally a literary form, influenced by French triomphe.
From Latin Trītōn.
From Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos).

parole.significato: trope (figure of speech in which words or phrases are used with a nonliteral or figurative meaning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tropus.
From New Latin Latin tragulus, diminutive of Latin tragus from Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “he-goat”).
Borrowed from Latin tripodem, from Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous).
Borrowed from Latin turba.
Borrowed from Latin Tantalus, from Ancient Greek Τάνταλος (Tántalos, “Tantalus”).
Borrowed from Latin taenia, from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “ribbon, tape”).
Learned borrowing from Latin topicus, from Ancient Greek τοπῐκός (topĭkós).
Borrowed from Latin toxicus, from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón).
From Latin uroborus, from Ancient Greek οὐροβόρος (ourobóros).
Inherited from Latin cichoria, plural of cichorium, a borrowing of Ancient Greek κιχόριον (kikhórion). The initial x is most like due to the influence of Mozarabic. Compare Spanish chicoria.
Borrowed from Latin zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos).
Borrowed from Latin zōdiācus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός (κύκλος) (zōidiakós (kúklos), literally “circle of little animals”), from ζῴδι(αι)ον (zōídi(ai)on), the diminutive of ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
Borrowed from Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē).

parole.significato: an abacus (calculating frame with beads constrained to rows by grooves or wires)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus, abax; from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “board or slab”).
From Latin achātēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs).
Borrowed from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē, “aloes”).
Borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús, “two handled jar”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ancora.
Borrowed from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós).
Borrowed from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”).
Borrowed from Latin aegidem, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́ς (aigĭ́s).

parole.significato: emphasis, force of expression or intonation to emphasize the importance of what is said or read
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis).

parole.significato: ether (the substance formerly supposed to fill the upper regions of the atmosphere above the clouds)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aethēr, from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr).
Borrowed from Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).

parole.significato: exodus (a sudden departure of a large number of people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos).
Borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon).
Borrowed from Latin orphicus, from Ancient Greek ορφικός (orphikós).
